classification.difficultyReason: Follow the scaffolded SSS and SAS proofs, then independently choose triangle pairs for the converse. The construction requires recognising equal-radius pairs as an implicit kite and transferring the perpendicular-diagonal result to the given line.

inlines.text: is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides. As with a rhombus, the properties of a kite are best seen when it is drawn in a diamond orientation, as in the diagram.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let $CFBG$ be a kite with $CF=CG$ and $BF=BG$. Let the diagonals $CB$ and $FG$ meet at $M$.

spec.description: Diamond-oriented kite with a longer upper portion, both diagonals, double upper-side ticks and triple lower-side ticks. No perpendicularity or diagonal-bisection marks are supplied.
spec.mathematics: CF=CG; BF=BG; M is the intersection of CB and FG.

answer.worked:
In triangles $CBF$ and $CBG$:
$$\begin{align*}CF&=CG&&\text{(given)}\\BF&=BG&&\text{(given)}\\CB&=CB&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle CBF\equiv\triangle CBG$ (SSS).

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence show that $CB$ bisects $\angle FCG$ and $\angle FBG$.

answer.short: $\angle FCB=\angle BCG$ and $\angle FBC=\angle CBG$, so $CB$ bisects both angles.
answer.worked:
Matching angles of the congruent triangles $CBF$ and $CBG$ give
$$\begin{align*}\angle FCB&=\angle BCG,\\\angle FBC&=\angle CBG.\end{align*}$$
Thus $CB$ bisects $\angle FCG$ and $\angle FBG$.

In triangles $CMF$ and $CMG$:
$$\begin{align*}CF&=CG&&\text{(given)}\\CM&=CM&&\text{(common)}\\\angle FCM&=\angle GCM&&\text{(part ii; }C,M,B\text{ are collinear)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle CMF\equiv\triangle CMG$ (SAS).

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence show that the diagonals are perpendicular.

answer.short: $CB\perp FG$: the equal adjacent angles at $M$ are each $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$\angle CMF=\angle CMG$ (matching angles of congruent triangles). Since $F,M,G$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle CMF+\angle CMG&=180^\circ,\\2\angle CMF&=180^\circ,\\\angle CMF&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $CB\perp FG$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Conversely, let $AFBG$ be a quadrilateral in which the diagonal $AB$ bisects the diagonal $FG$ and is perpendicular to it. Prove that $AFBG$ is a kite.

spec.description: Quadrilateral AFBG with AB vertical, FG horizontal, equal FM and MG marks and a right-angle square between MA and MG.
spec.mathematics: FM=MG; AB is perpendicular to FG at M. AM and BM are not marked equal.

answer.short:
$AF=AG$ and $BF=BG$, so $AFBG$ is a kite.

Use SAS on the two pairs of triangles meeting at $M$.
answer.worked:
Since $AB$ bisects $FG$ at right angles, $FM=GM$ and all four angles at $M$ are right angles.

In triangles $AMF$ and $AMG$:
$$\begin{align*}FM&=GM&&\text{(given)}\\\angle AMF&=\angle AMG=90^\circ,\\AM&=AM&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AMF\equiv\triangle AMG$ (SAS), so $AF=AG$.

In triangles $BMF$ and $BMG$:
$$\begin{align*}FM&=GM&&\text{(given)}\\\angle BMF&=\angle BMG=90^\circ,\\BM&=BM&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BMF\equiv\triangle BMG$ (SAS), so $BF=BG$.

Thus $AFBG$ has two pairs of equal adjacent sides and is a kite.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Let $\ell$ be a line and $P$ a point not on the line. Choose two points $A$ and $B$ on $\ell$. Draw an arc with centre $A$ and radius $AP$. Then draw a second arc with centre $B$ and radius $BP$. Let the arcs meet at $M$. Explain why $PM$ is perpendicular to $\ell$.

spec.description: Two arcs with distinct centres A and B on line ell meet at P and M. Their radii differ. The constructed PM line is dashed red; A, B and P have red point markers. No right-angle mark is added.
spec.mathematics: AP=AM and BP=BM; A and B lie on ell; P and M are the two common arc intersections.
spec.answerVisibility: Construction givens are visible; no proof or additional equality marks are supplied.

answer.short: $AP=AM$ and $BP=BM$, so $APBM$ is a kite. Its diagonals $PM$ and $AB$ are perpendicular; hence $PM\perp\ell$.
answer.worked:
$AP=AM$ because both are radii of the circle with centre $A$. Likewise $BP=BM$ because both are radii of the circle with centre $B$.

Thus $APBM$ is a kite. By part a, its diagonals $AB$ and $PM$ are perpendicular. Since $A$ and $B$ lie on $\ell$, $PM\perp\ell$.
